item.title: Iran rules out nuclear site inspections until war ends
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: A senior Iranian official said Sunday that Tehran will not allow International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to return to examine damaged nuclear facilities until the war has "permanently ended." IAEA inspectors visited Iran's Bushehr nuclear plant in September but have not gained access to other sites targeted by the U.S. since the war started.Yemen's Houthi rebels have forced government-allied forces to pull back from areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Iran-backed Houthis have fought for months to consolidate their control over the waterway - a key route for Saudi oil and gas exports.Hostilities around the Persian Gulf have also increased in recent days, with attacks on commercial vessels continuing and Iran claiming another attack targeting a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain. Bahraini officials said the weapons were intercepted, and the U.S. military denied a similar claim from Iran late last week.
New Updates
16m ago
Iran reportedly claims Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes endorsed by U.S. are "fully mined"
A Saudi news outlet closely linked to the government and ruling royal family cited Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as claiming Monday that southern shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz, which the Trump administration and U.S. military have insisted are safe and open, have been "fully mined."
There was no immediate statement from the IRGC itself echoing the report by Saudi Arabia's Asharq News, which is not technically state-run, but owned by a state-backed institution in the kingdom.

item.title: U.K. mulls changing sexual consent laws after Russell Brand case
item.description:
London — Britain's government is considering changing the U.K.'s laws on the legal age of sexual consent as a woman who claims she was raped by convicted sex offender Russell Brand campaigns to criminalize sex between adults and 16- or 17-year-olds.
British Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said over the weekend that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" had emerged last week, warranting consideration of a new law that would set out different ages of consent depending on the ages of the individuals involved.
Already practiced by several other nations, the merits of this staggered age of consent approach have "been raised and will be discussed" by the government, McFadden said, adding that he "can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."
A day after Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault, fellow British television personality and author David Walliams was named as the subject of multiple allegations of grooming young girls and harassing female colleagues.
British comedian and actor Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London on Nov. 5, 2026.
Zeynep Demir/Anadolu via Getty Images
Under current U.K. law, an adult of any age can have sex with a consenting person 16 years old or older. If a staggered system were imposed, it could make it illegal for anyone 18 or older, for instance, to have sex with individuals aged between 16 and 18, regardless of whether they gave verbal consent.

item.title: Trump heads to Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
item.description:
Washington — President Trump is setting off Monday for a multi-day swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
Ahead of his departure, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.
The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first between the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.
Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.
The president will first head to the Philippines, where the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is being held. Mr. Trump will meet with Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.
On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, mar...

item.title: Drawing China close, is Kim Jong Un bracing to confront the U.S.?
item.description:
Dandong, China — With a pair of binoculars and a camera hanging around his neck, retired Chinese government official Mr. Yang leaned against a fence on a boardwalk that meanders through the city of Dandong, peering across the wide Yalu River that separates China from North Korea.
He came to visit from Dalian, about 200 miles away, despite the temperature hovering just above freezing, to catch a glimpse of life inside China's heavily sanctioned, nuclear armed neighbor nation. But the main attraction he came to see is the massive new bridge towering over Dandong, which now links the two countries.
"The bridge is good, but it's only for trucks and cars, not for the trains," he complained. "But this is good for trade, and I do hope this means relations improve with North Korea."
At almost two miles long and four lanes across, the new Yalu River Bridge is a feat of engineering. The Chinese side was finished 12 years ago, but North Korea only recently completed its section, with leader Kim Jong Un making a surprise appearance for the official opening on Oct. 24.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, alongside Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, takes part in the opening of the new Yalu River Bridge, Oct. 24, 2026.
Rao Aimin/Xinhua via AP
As CBS News visited the new river crossing, a large group of tourists arrived from Fujian province, more than 1,000 miles to the south, to pose for photos in front of the impressive piece of infrastructure.
"This will enhance the friendship between China and North Korea for sure, but we hope that North Korea will open up to the West," tour group leader Mr. Sun told CBS News. "North Korea was an isolated country, and this shows they're trying to join the world."

item.title: Women in U.K. are getting automatic pardons for past abortion convictions
item.description:
Women in the United Kingdom who were convicted of illegally terminating their pregnancies under a Victorian-era law will receive automatic pardons on Monday, the government said.
This follows the passage of a landmark vote by Parliament last year to decriminalize abortion by repealing a section of the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act.
Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned, and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records. They will not have to apply for pardons, and some will be issued posthumously.
The government did not provide the number of women affected. But Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour member of Parliament who introduced the decriminalization amendment, said police have investigated more than 100 women suspected of illegal abortions in the five years preceding last year's vote. That included some who suffered natural miscarriages and stillbirths.
Antoniazzi described how women suspected of illegally aborting a fetus were once "dragged from hospital beds to police cells" and interrogated when they should have been cared for.
"This trauma cannot be erased, but I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they've always wanted to," she said.
Under current law, doctors can legally carry out abortions in England, Scotland and Wales up to 24 weeks, and beyond that under special circumstances, such as when the life of the mother is in danger. Abortion in Northern Ireland was decriminalized in 2019.
Under the Crime and Policing Act that took effect this spring, women who terminate a pregnancy at any stage will not face criminal charges.
The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.

item.title: Trump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
item.description:
Washington — President Trump said he may meet with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un during his trip to Asia this week.
As he left the White House Monday morning for a summit in the Philippines, which will be followed by a trip to China, Mr. Trump told reporters the meeting with Kim would take place in China — if it happens. No meeting with Kim has been confirmed by the White House. The president said whether the meeting happens is up to Chinese President Xi Jinping. Mr. Trump will meet with Xi, along with Russian President Vladimir Putin, later this week.
"We'll be with President Xi," the president told reporters on the White House South Lawn. "He was here a month ago. And we're also going to meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un, also. So that'll be good. We could — we have a chance to accomplish a lot."
The president said he doesn't know if Kim will come.
"He may come," Mr. Trump said of Kim. "I don't know. That's up to President Xi."
Mr. Trump has met with the North Korean leader in person three times, all during his first term in office. He is the only sitting U.S. president to have met with Kim.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

item.title: Drug lord who orchestrated murder of U.S. agent dies at 80
item.description:
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking known as "the boss of bosses," who transformed the global cocaine trade and orchestrated the murder of a U.S. agent, died Sunday at age 80, officials said.
The notorious drug kingpin, a former police officer who played a key role in forging alliances with Colombian traffickers, died in a hospital where he had been transferred from prison two days earlier.
"After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility" after "he suffered multiple organ failure," according to a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.
Felix Gallardo's health had deteriorated markedly in recent years, with conditions including high blood pressure, diabetes and deafness.
In 2022, then-president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said he was "in very poor health." A judge granted him house arrest, but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer.
One of the founders of the Guadalajara cartel, from which the Sinaloa cartel would later emerge, Felix Gallardo had been incarcerated since 1989 and was serving a 40-year sentence.
He was convicted for the 1985 murder of an undercover U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency officer, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena Salazar, which outraged the United States. Last year, Camarena's alleged killer, Rafael Caro Quintero, was transferred to the U.S. along with 28 other prisoners requested by the U.S. government.
Camarena, a father of three sons, was living in Guadalajara, Mexico, with his family working as an undercover DEA agent, his son told CBS News in a 2017 interview. He had been stationed there for four years on the trail of the country's biggest marijuana and cocaine traffickers.

item.title: Basketball player allegedly had 75 pounds of drugs in luggage
item.description:
Nigeria's anti-narcotics agency on Sunday said it had arrested an American professional basketball player with 33.95 kilograms (about 75 pounds) of cannabis in his luggage on arrival at the main airport.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) named the player as 28-year-old Greene Da'monte Khiree, a native of Savannah, Georgia.
He was arrested on Wednesday at the main international airport car park in Lagos after he "was observed abandoning his two checked-in bags before attempting to exit the airport with only his carry-on luggage," NDLEA said in a statement.
The bags bearing his name tags were filled with 16 packs of Loud, described as a "potent strain of cannabis," said NDLEA, which posted several images of the player with suitcases full of the purported drugs.
Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said the player was 28-year-old Greene Da'monte Khiree.
National Drug Law Enforcement Agency
He had arrived in Lagos from Thailand, where he said he had lived and played professional basketball since October 2025, the agency said.
The agency said he claimed he was visiting Nigeria to "build networks for his basketball career" but examination of his mobile phone showed information suggesting his "knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity."
FIBA lists a player by the name DaMonte Greene, a point guard, one of whose recent appearances was at the Phuket Elite Cup in September.
Greene was the leading scorer for the semiprofessional Georgia Bombers during the 2023-24 season, averaging 26.3 points per game, according to the Basketball Job Market.

item.title: Bahrain says it intercepted Iranian strikes, Tehran targets U.S. assets
item.description:
Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Monday, November 16, here. See earlier developments below.
What to know about the Iran war: Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said their forces carried out a drone attack on a U.S. radar system at a base in Bahrain early Sunday, according to a state broadcaster. Bahrain later said it had intercepted Iranian strikes. The country was repeatedly targeted by Iran in the opening months of the war in retaliation for U.S. strikes, but has not registered major attacks since September.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a speech about forming a unity government with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, invoked the possibility of Iran developing nuclear weapons and said it was time to end the threat "once and for all."Three oil tankers struck mines overnight and were on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps. They did not provide the names of the ships and the strikes could not be verified.
